subject: Chefs 1974 to 2013: Michael Roussel and Lazone Randolph
fact: (search: Times-Picayune obituary mirrored on groups.google.com) Michael J. Roussel died in July 2005 aged 67, having retired earlier that year after 49 years at Brennan's, the last 30 as executive chef; he apprenticed under Paul Blangé and became executive chef in 1974. (search: cooksinfo.com, southernfoodways.org) Paul Blangé, 1900 to 1977, created Bananas Foster, Eggs Hussarde and Chicken Pontalba. (search: frenchquarterly.com, brennansrestaurant.blogspot.com, bizneworleans.com) Lazone Randolph started as a dishwasher in 1965, was named executive chef in 2005 succeeding Roussel, and is the chef behind Chicken Lazone. (pdf p49) The guide names only Blangé and Kris Padalino. The first pass's correction erred twice: Roussel did not die in post, and he became executive chef in 1974, before Blangé's death. 49 years back from 2005 gives a 1956 start.
forThePack: Paul Blangé, the chef behind Bananas Foster, led the kitchen until the 1970s. Michael Roussel, who started here in 1956 and trained under Blangé, became executive chef in 1974 and retired in 2005 after 49 years. Lazone Randolph, who began as a dishwasher in 1965, succeeded him in 2005 and gave his name to Chicken Lazone. Chef Kris Padalino has led the kitchen since June 2025.

subject: Louisiana Oysters, p10: the Worcestershire clause
fact: (search: brennansneworleans.com breakfast and lunch menu) Louisiana Oysters with New Orleans BBQ Sauce, pickled collard greens, shallots and fried saltine crumble at $19, matching p10 word for word; the menu says nothing about Worcestershire. (pdf p10, p11) Butter, black pepper and Worcestershire is given as the definition of the barbecue shrimp style, not the house recipe; the service note flags the anchovy in Worcestershire and says confirm the sauce at lineup. (expert) That is the standard Pascal's Manale style description, so the clause is a style note and the first pass's correction stands.
forThePack: New Orleans barbecue is not a smoker or a tomato sauce: it is the buttery, peppery style made famous by barbecue shrimp. Our Louisiana Oysters come in that sauce with pickled collard greens, shallots and a fried saltine crumble. If a guest asks what exactly is in the sauce, or about Worcestershire or anchovy, check with the kitchen.

subject: Fresno chilli, p13
fact: (search: pepperscale.com, chilipeppermadness.com) Fresno runs 2,500 to 10,000 Scoville and jalapeño 2,500 to 8,000; green Fresnos average about 3,200 and red about 7,100. (search: en.wikipedia.org) Developed by Clarence Brown Hamlin in 1952, named for Fresno, California, thinner walls, matures faster; the article says often milder. Same band as a jalapeño, a red one a touch hotter, the real difference being the thinner wall and fruitier flavour. (pdf p13) 'Tangy with just a gentle warmth' is the honest table description of the preserved chilli in the mignonette.
forThePack: Fresno is a red Californian chilli from the 1950s, about the heat of a jalapeño but fruitier and thinner walled. Preserved and stirred into the mignonette it gives a gentle warmth, not real heat.

subject: Creole turtle soup canon: Commander's Palace and the veal
fact: (search: foodnetwork.com, cdkitchen.com, louisiana.kitchenandculture.com) The published Commander's Palace turtle soup uses equal parts turtle, veal stew meat and lean beef, with trinity, tomato puree, Worcestershire, beef stock, a light brown roux, lemon, chopped hard cooked eggs, spinach and sherry. (search: nomenu.com) Tom Fitzmorris says the regional style descends from Commander's and is distinctive in using as much veal shoulder as turtle. So the original claim was sound and the first pass's correction (turtle cooked in veal stock, not equal parts) was wrong. (search: en.wikipedia.org, 64parishes.org) Prudhomme became Commander's executive chef in 1975, so mid 1970s. (search: brennansneworleans.com/recipes/turtle-soup, saveur.com) Brennan's own recipe is turtle only. (pdf p14) '100% turtle meat, brown butter spinach, grated egg, aged Sherry'. (expert) That the menu line is a deliberate contrast with Commander's is an inference nobody at Brennan's has stated.
forThePack: Many New Orleans turtle soups, including the famous one at Commander's Palace, stretch the turtle with veal and beef. Ours is 100 percent turtle meat, with brown butter spinach, grated egg and a splash of aged Sherry at the end. Do not say ours was written against any other restaurant's recipe; confirm the house recipe at lineup before saying more.

subject: Eggs Sardou
fact: (pdf p18) The name goes back to the playwright Victorien Sardou; Brennan's build is crispy artichokes, poached eggs, Parmesan creamed spinach, Choron. (search: saveur.com, en.wikipedia.org, chowhound.com) Created at Antoine's, usually dated 1908, for Sardou: poached eggs on artichoke bottoms with anchovies, hollandaise, minced black truffle, parsley and ham, served with fried asparagus spears; most versions today use creamed spinach. The first pass was right that the original had no spinach but wrong to drop the asparagus. (search: mission-food.com) Brennan's swaps hollandaise for Choron. (expert) Antoine Alciatore died in 1877, so say 'at Antoine's' and name no cook; 1908 is lore, not record.
forThePack: Eggs Sardou was created at Antoine's, usually dated 1908, for the French playwright Victorien Sardou. The original was poached eggs on artichoke bottoms with hollandaise, anchovy, ham and truffle, with no spinach. The creamed spinach most kitchens use now came later. Ours fries the artichokes, makes the spinach with Parmesan and swaps hollandaise for Choron, a béarnaise with tomato.

subject: Débris
fact: (pdf p19, p50) Débris, DAY-bree, is slow-cooked meat that falls apart into its own gravy; no origin given. (search: mothersrestaurant.net/history) Simon and Mary Landry opened Mother's at 401 Poydras in 1938, and the restaurant's own history says Simon Landry coined the term when a customer asked for the bits of roast beef that fell into the gravy. (search: nolaeats.com) Mother's has the strongest documented claim to the word for New Orleans roast beef. The first pass was wrong to strike Landry personally and right that 'coined' is the restaurant's story. (expert) Débris is ordinary Louisiana French for scraps and Cajun kitchens used it before 1938, so say popularised, not invented.
forThePack: Débris, DAY-bree, is the New Orleans word for the shreds of slow-cooked meat that fall into their own gravy. Mother's on Poydras Street, open since 1938, made the word famous: its story is that founder Simon Landry asked a customer whether he wanted 'some of the debris' from the roast beef carving board. Ours is short rib braised in red wine until it falls apart.

subject: Sauce Foyot
fact: (pdf p24, p50) Béarnaise enriched with reduced meat glaze, fwah-YO. (search: fr.wikipedia.org, Escoffier on fr.wikisource) Also called sauce Valois; Escoffier prints it as 'Sauce Béarnaise à la glace de viande, dite Foyot, ou Valois' in 1903 and 1934; named for Nicolas Foyot and his restaurant opposite the Senate. (search: en.wikipedia.org Restaurant Foyot, parismuseescollections.paris.fr) The Restaurant Foyot at 33 rue de Tournon closed in 1937 after 169 years; Nicolas Foyot, chef to Louis-Philippe, bought it after 1848; Léopold Mourier succeeded him in 1891. The first pass's correction was right on the sauce, the synonym and the address, and right to strike Gouffé and 1863; it erred in calling Foyot the founder and in saying 1938. (expert) Whether Foyot or Mourier first made the sauce is not settled.
forThePack: Sauce Foyot, fwah-YO, is béarnaise made richer with a reduced meat glaze; Escoffier lists it as Foyot or Valois. It is named for the Restaurant Foyot, which stood on the rue de Tournon opposite the Senate in Paris until 1937 and took its name from Nicolas Foyot, once chef to King Louis-Philippe, who bought the house after 1848.

subject: Luxardo
fact: (pdf p34) The Italian house famous for maraschino cherries and liqueur. (search: imbibemagazine.com, en.wikipedia.org) Girolamo Luxardo founded the distillery in 1821 in Zara, now Zadar in Croatia, from the rosolio maraschino his wife Maria Canevari made at home; after 1945 the company moved to Torreglia near Padua and Giorgio Luxardo restarted it in 1947 with marasca plants from a Florence botanist. The first pass's correction is confirmed, including 1947 rather than 1946. (expert) The orchards are usually quoted at around 30,000 trees; the snippets do not confirm the count.
forThePack: Luxardo is the Italian house famous for maraschino. It was founded in 1821 in Zara, now Zadar in Croatia, by Girolamo Luxardo from the rosolio maraschino his wife Maria Canevari made at home. The distillery was lost in the Second World War, and the family restarted it in 1947 at Torreglia near Padua, where it grows its own marasca cherries.

subject: Bread pudding origin
fact: (pdf p35) New Orleans' comfort dessert; Brennan's build is whiskey caramel, buttermilk ice cream and pralines. (search: myneworleans.com, ckbk.com) The 1901 Picayune's Creole Cook Book pain perdu calls for eggs, sugar, stale bread, orange flower water, grated lemon zest and brandy, so the claim's list was right and the first pass was wrong to doubt the zest; the same book has a separate Pouding de Pain with diced stale bread, eggs, milk, sugar, raisins and lemon or vanilla, so the first pass was right that pain perdu is not the bread pudding anchor. (search: gumbopages.com, ckbk.com) The Bon Ton Café, revived in the early 1950s by Al and Alzina Pierce, made the whiskey sauce bread pudding famous. (expert) The medieval European thrift origin is the safe wording; the 11th to 12th century and 18th century New Orleans dates are weakly sourced.
forThePack: Bread pudding is an old European thrift dish for stale bread that became a New Orleans staple; the Picayune's Creole Cook Book of 1901 already prints a baked bread pudding with raisins and custard. The warm whiskey sauce is a 20th-century New Orleans restaurant signature, made famous at the Bon Ton Café. Ours takes it a step further with a whiskey caramel, buttermilk ice cream and pralines.

subject: Brabant potatoes: name, Picayune citation, method, Louisiana fries
fact: (search: americastestkitchen.com, ckbk.com) The Picayune Creole Cook Book (1901) includes Brabant Potatoes, Pommes de Terre Brabant, parboiled cubes skillet fried in butter and lard, so the citation is real and earlier than the claim's 1922; cite 1901 or early 1900s. (search: americastestkitchen.com, sprinklesandsprouts.com) Named for the Brabant region, a former duchy now divided between the Netherlands and Belgium; the claim's 'northern France' rests on one blog line and is wrong. (search: deepsouthdish.com) 'Louisiana fries' is a food blog nickname. (pdf p30, p31) Cubes fried golden and crisp, finished with garlic, butter and parsley, bra-BAHNT; the garlic finish is the modern restaurant version. (expert) Lemon is not standard.
sources: app.ckbk.com Brabant Potatoes, The Picayune's Creole Cook Book
forThePack: Brabant potatoes are an old New Orleans restaurant side, in the Picayune's Creole Cook Book since the early 1900s and named for the Brabant region of Belgium and the Netherlands. Cubes of potato fried golden and crisp, fluffy inside, finished with garlic butter and parsley. Say bra-BAHNT. Do not say northern France, 1922 or Louisiana fries; confirm the kitchen's finish and fryer.

(search: iba-world.com) The IBA recipe is 50 ml Cognac, 10 ml absinthe, sugar cube, 2 dashes Peychaud's, stirred and strained into an absinthe rinsed glass, with the note that rye replaced Cognac after the Civil War; so the claim's 'cognac or rye' overstates the IBA. (pdf p39) Brennan's prints Sazerac rye, Peychaud's and a Herbsaint rinse, stirred, up, with no sugar or peel printed, so the bar's build must be confirmed.

The Sazerac Company's own recipe is a sugar cube, three dashes of Peychaud's, an ounce and a half of Sazerac Rye, a quarter ounce of Herbsaint and a lemon peel, built across two glasses; the IBA version is Cognac based with absinthe. Give those as the classic, never as the house build.

subject: Banyuls AOC rules: grapes, mutage, alcohol, Grand Cru
fact: (search: INAO cahier des charges Banyuls via lespassionnesduvin.com and hachette-vins.com) Banyuls and Banyuls Grand Cru are vins doux naturels whose fermentation is stopped by mutage with neutral grape spirit of at least 96 percent at 5 to 10 percent of the must volume; Grenache noir must be at least 50 percent of a Banyuls blend. (search: INAO cahier des charges Banyuls Grand Cru, inao.gouv.fr) Grand Cru requires Grenache noir at 75 percent or more and at least 30 months under wood, recognised by decree of 16 November 1962; a trade page saying 70 percent is overridden by the INAO text. The claim's 'half Grenache (noir, gris, blanc)' is wrong on the grape: the floor is Grenache noir alone. (expert) The finished wine is usually 15 to 18 percent alcohol. (pdf p46) Grenache, fortified, Roussillon; the Reserva is an oxidative style.
forThePack: Banyuls is a sweet fortified red, a vin doux naturel, from the schist terraces around Banyuls-sur-Mer in Roussillon, French Catalonia. It must be at least half Grenache noir, and fermentation is stopped with neutral grape spirit so the grape's own sugar stays in the wine. Banyuls Grand Cru is at least three quarters Grenache noir and spends at least thirty months in wood. Our pour is the La Tour Vieille Reserva: fig, caramel, cocoa and coffee, the classic with chocolate.

subject: C.H. Berres Old Vines Riesling: dry or off-dry
fact: (search: thesortingtable.com importer page for the 2022) C.H. Berres Estate Riesling Old Vines Mosel 2022 carries 20.7 g/l residual sugar at 11.5 percent alcohol and the winemaker's note calls it 'a rich and modern, semi-sweet Riesling'; the 2021 carried 18.9 g/l. So the wine is off-dry to semi-sweet, not dry, and the p6 line 'off-dry-leaning' is the nearest the guide comes to right. (pdf p4, p16, p20, p42) The hedges stay in the text, so the guide is inconsistent rather than silent, but the open question is settled. (expert) Residual sugar moves with the vintage, so taste the open bottle at lineup.
sources: guide.txt p4, p6, p16, p20, p42
forThePack: The Berres Old Vines Riesling is off-dry: a touch of sweetness, about twenty grams of sugar a litre, with only 11.5% alcohol and racy Mosel acidity. That is why it is our glass for spice and for the maple on the duck. Taste it at lineup if the vintage has changed.

subject: Turtle Soup and the Piper-Heidsieck Extra Brut: toast against the aged Sherry
fact: (search: piper-heidsieck.com technical sheet, libertywines.co.uk) Essentiel Extra Brut is 44 percent Pinot Noir, 34 Meunier, 22 Chardonnay with 23 percent reserve wine, at least 36 months on lees and 6 g/l dosage; notes of plum, brioche, grapefruit, acacia honey and toasted nuts. (search: jjbuckley.com, flatiron-wines.com) Rare 2012 is 70 percent Chardonnay, 30 Pinot Noir, with grilled almonds, candied orange peel, brioche and roasted hazelnut. The NV's toast comes from long lees ageing, Rare carries the nut and candied citrus more fully, and neither is oxidative. (pdf p14, p15) The guide leads with dryness and bubbles and keeps Rare as the closer match. The guide spells the house pour 'Essential'; the producer's cuvée is Essentiel.
forThePack: Our house Champagne is Piper-Heidsieck's Extra Brut: at least three years on the lees and only about six grams of sugar, so it is bone dry, with brioche and toasted nut from that long ageing that pick up the Sherry in the turtle soup while the bubbles clear the richness. For a step up, Rare 2012 is seventy percent Chardonnay with grilled almond and candied orange that meet the Sherry even more closely.
